evidence_set: The commentary critiques the review of vaping by Banks and colleagues funded by the Australian Department of Health, citing the 2022 report to the Department (reference 1; the 2023 article read for this claim is based on it and appeared later). In the authors' view the review failed its aims because it did not compare the relative risk of the harms of vaping with those of cigarettes, did not consider the net public health impact, ignored evidence that vaping is effective for stopping smoking, and confused causation and correlation in reading the link between youth vaping and later smoking; and it applied different standards of evidence to the two questions, accepting a causal reading of observational associations for starting to smoke while rejecting similar observational evidence on quitting and treating trials that found vaping helps people quit with scepticism. The authors say they summarise evidence inconsistent with the review's main findings; they describe no search and no formal appraisal of their sources. These criticisms concern the question asked, the comparison and the standards of evidence, not new measurements of disease.

On heart and lung outcomes the commentary cites no study of how often heart attack, stroke or chronic lung disease occur in people who vape, and it agrees that human studies on cardiovascular outcomes are limited; it states that most cardiovascular effects of vaping are consistent with those of nicotine (transiently raised pulse and blood pressure, cardiac contractility, arrhythmogenesis) and that nicotine may pose some risk in people with existing cardiovascular disease. Its evidence of benefit concerns people who switched from smoking: sustained falls in blood pressure (two studies), better vascular function after 4 weeks (one study), and improved respiratory symptoms, lung function, asthma, COPD, mucociliary clearance and fewer infections, with seven of the nine human studies or reviews it cites sharing authors (references 35, 36 and 38 to 42, by the author lists printed). The review rated changes after switching in people with asthma, bronchitis or COPD as insufficient evidence and clinical cardiovascular outcomes as no available evidence (anchors above), so the two weigh the same small body of switching studies differently and do not disagree about disease rates, which neither has.

On the 2019 US lung-injury outbreak (EVALI), the authors call a causal role for nicotine vaping highly implausible: they say the outbreak was strongly linked to vitamin E acetate added to illicit THC vaping oils and disappeared after its removal from the illicit supply (CDC, reference 46), and that the 14% of patients who denied using THC and had vaped nicotine do not prove a causal link with nicotine vaping products, because many patients who denied vaping THC were later found to have done so and no other causal agent has been identified in nicotine e-liquids (references 47 and 48; no numbers given). The review's own wording is a causal link largely for THC-containing products, with 14% of cases in its largest study reporting only nicotine products (anchor above), so the disagreement is about how far self-reported product use can be trusted.

On cancer, the commentary cites an estimate that lifetime cancer risk from vaping is less than 0.5% of that from smoking, derived from the reduced number and dose of carcinogens in vapour (references 49 and 50, which by their titles estimate risk from emissions and particle measurements; not read), and the Cochrane review's finding of no evidence of harm in its few studies of up to 2 years. Neither is a measured rate of cancer in people who vape, and the estimate's comparison is with smoking, not with using no nicotine; the review rated invasive cancer as no available evidence (anchor above).

evidence_set: On the meeting's funding and membership, as the authors report it: one sponsor, a company called EuroSwiss Health, is one of several companies registered at one address near Geneva with the same chief executive, who is reported to have received funding from British American Tobacco for a book on nicotine as harm reduction (the book states that its conclusions were developed independently of the company) and who endorsed that company's public health credentials in its 2013 sustainability report; a supporting organisation, Lega Italiana Anti Fumo, had as chief scientific adviser one of the 12 attendees, who declared funding from an e-cigarette manufacturer but not funding he is reported elsewhere to have received from Philip Morris International. The rationale for choosing the panel is not given; it included several known e-cigarette advocates, some declaring industry funding in the paper, and some people not known for expertise in tobacco control; Public Health England's tobacco lead attended. The authors quote the paper's statement that the sponsor had no role in any stage of the process or in the writing and was not present at the workshop. The ties are sourced to a company register entry, two Tobacco Tactics web pages, the book and a company report (none read) and are worded as reported; the article does not claim that they changed the ratings. Recorded as a reason to read the 2014 paper closely, not as evidence about harm.

The authors argue that where risks are uncertain the precautionary principle should apply, so that, without scientific consensus that a substance is not harmful to the public, the burden of proof lies with those taking an action; that the report's headline message, widely quoted in the media, that best estimates show e-cigarettes to be 95% less harmful to health than cigarettes seemingly left little room for uncertainty about long-term risks; and that the report did not cite a 2014 systematic review (Pisinger and Døssing, reference 11, not read) that found serious methodological problems in many of its 76 studies, a third (34%) published by authors with conflicts of interest, and concluded that no firm conclusions on safety could be drawn, while adding that e-cigarettes could hardly be considered free of harm.

The authors describe two sides that compare with different references: supporters focus on people who already smoke and compare e-cigarettes with smoking, while those concerned about uptake by people who would not otherwise smoke and about long-term effects argue that, although e-cigarettes lack some of the most harmful substances in cigarettes, such as tar, they contain others, such as formaldehyde (a carcinogen) and diverse flavourings, so non-smoking should also be a comparison. They add that reduced smoking, as opposed to quitting, may not lower the overall risk of death (a 16-year Copenhagen cohort of 19,732 people, reference 8, not read); that two thirds of people who use e-cigarettes also smoke (no source given), a pattern the 2015 report rarely mentions; and that in one cohort dual use among people who vaped daily apparently stayed above 80% after 12 months of follow-up (reference 9, not read).

The authors state that none of the research so far (in context, on youth uptake and a gateway to smoking) can be considered conclusive and longer-term studies are needed; that the report seemed to equate a lack of evidence of risk to bystanders with evidence of no effect; that it omitted the lack of evidence on the risks of long-term dual use; that perhaps its most striking feature was a consistent adoption of the most optimistic position on limited evidence; and they agree with England's chief medical officer that evidence on the long-term use of e-cigarettes is still lacking. Key messages: Public Health England's endorsement of the safety and efficacy of e-cigarettes rests on uncertain evidence, and public health strategies should follow the precautionary principle until better evidence is available. The article offers no estimate of its own of how much less harmful e-cigarettes are than cigarettes, presents no new data, does not discuss measurements of toxicant exposure or short-term health measures in people who switched from smoking, and reports no reply from the authors of the 2015 report or of the 2014 paper. The National Academies' summary of its concerns (the National Academies anchor above) matches its themes, except relapse, which the article does not mention.

The authors argue that the key public health question is the net population effect, which depends on the harm difference between vaping and smoking, on effectiveness for stopping smoking and on uptake by people who do and do not smoke; they report that numerous modelling studies, with one exception, conclude that benefits considerably exceed harms (one US model, under current patterns of vaping and substitution: 1.8 million premature smoking- and vaping-attributable deaths avoided and 38.9 million life-years gained from 2013 to 2060). As they describe them, these models evaluate net effects under a wide range of assumptions about the reduction in harm compared with smoking, so they take the size of the difference as an input rather than measuring it (editors' reading). None of the models was read.
